on each object, so we can alternatively write
(\beta\circ\alpha)(\rho)=\big(\beta(-)\bullet\alpha(-)\big)\circ\mathord{\hbox{\hbox to8.85pt{\vbox to10.6pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 4.42474pt\lower-2.37526pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

\lxSVG@closescope }}}
{{}}{}
{{}{}}{{{{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}}}}{{}}{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 2.11 L 0 -3.01}{fill:none} \ignorespaces
{{}}{}
{{}{}}{{{{{}}{}{}{}{}{{}}}}}{{}}{}{}{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 2.22 7.48 L 5.85 11.1}{fill:none} \ignorespaces

\lxSVG@closescope {\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}{\ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\circ\rho
. Note that we indicate composition in
\mathcal{C}
by
\bullet
and composition in the fibres
\mathsf{Stat}(X)
by
\circ
.

Example 3.2
.

Let
\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{Meas}
be a ‘convenient’ (
i.e.
, Cartesian closed) category of measurable spaces, such as the category of quasi-Borel spaces
[
18
]
, let
\mathcal{P}:\mathbf{Meas}\to\mathbf{Meas}
be a probability monad defined on this category, and let
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})
be the Kleisli category of this monad. Its objects are the objects of
\mathbf{Meas}
, and its hom-spaces
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(A,B)
are the spaces
\mathbf{Meas}(A,\mathcal{P}B)

[
8
]
. This
\mathcal{C}
is a monoidal category of stochastic channels, whose monoidal unit
I
is the space with a single point. Consequently, states of
X
are just measures (distributions) in
\mathcal{P}X
. That is,
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(I,X)\cong\mathbf{Meas}(1,\mathcal{P}X)
. Instantiating
\mathsf{Stat}
in this setting, we obtain:

\displaystyle\mathsf{Stat}\;\;:\;\;\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})\op\;

\displaystyle\to\;\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}

\displaystyle X

\displaystyle\mapsto\mathsf{Stat}(X):=\quad\begin{pmatrix}[l]&\mathsf{Stat}(X)_{0}&:=\quad\;\;\;\mathbf{Meas}_{0}\\
&\mathsf{Stat}(X)(A,B)&:=\quad\;\;\;\mathbf{Meas}(\mathcal{P}X,\mathbf{Meas}(A,\mathcal{P}B))\\
\id_{A}\>:&\mathsf{Stat}(X)(A,A)&:=\quad\left\{\begin{aligned} \id_{A}:&\;\mathcal{P}X\to\mathbf{Meas}(A,\mathcal{P}A)\\
&\;\;\;\rho\;\;\,\mapsto\quad\eta_{A}\end{aligned}\right.\\
\end{pmatrix}

(17)

\displaystyle c:\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(Y,X)

\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}[c]\mathsf{Stat}(c)\;:&\mathsf{Stat}(X)&\to&\mathsf{Stat}(Y)\vskip 5.0pt\\
&\mathsf{Stat}(X)_{0}&=&\mathsf{Stat}(Y)_{0}\vskip 5.0pt\\
&\begin{pmatrix}[l]d^{\dagger}:&\mathcal{P}X&\to\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(A,B)\\
&\;\pi&\mapsto\quad\quad d^{\dagger}_{\pi}\end{pmatrix}&\mapsto&\begin{pmatrix}c^{\ast}d^{\dagger}:\mathcal{P}Y\to\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(A,B)\\
\rho\quad\mapsto\quad d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\rho}\end{pmatrix}\end{pmatrix}

Each
\mathsf{Stat}(X)
is a category of stochastic channels with respect to measures on the space
X
. We can write morphisms
d^{\dagger}:\mathcal{P}X\to\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(A,B)
in
\mathsf{Stat}(X)
as
d^{\dagger}_{(\cdot)}:A\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\xrightarrow{(\cdot)}$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\xrightarrow{(\cdot)}$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\xrightarrow{(\cdot)}$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\xrightarrow{(\cdot)}$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}B
, and think of them as generalized Bayesian inversions: given a measure
\pi
on
X
, we obtain a channel
d^{\dagger}_{\pi}:A\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\pi}$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\xrightarrow{\pi}$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\xrightarrow{\pi}$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\xrightarrow{\pi}$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}B
with respect to
\pi
. Given a channel
c:Y\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
in the base category of priors, we can pull
d^{\dagger}
back along
c
, to obtain a
Y\text{-dependent}
channel in
\mathsf{Stat}(Y)
,
c^{\ast}d^{\dagger}:\mathcal{P}Y\to\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(A,B)
, which takes
\rho:\mathcal{P}Y
to the channel
d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\rho}:A\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\xrightarrow{c\bullet\rho}$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\xrightarrow{c\bullet\rho}$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\xrightarrow{c\bullet\rho}$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\xrightarrow{c\bullet\rho}$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}B
defined by pushing
\rho
through
c
and then applying
d^{\dagger}
.

Remark 3.3
.

Note that by taking
\mathbf{Meas}
to be Cartesian closed, we have
\mathbf{Meas}(\mathcal{P}X,\mathbf{Meas}(A,\mathcal{P}B))\cong\mathbf{Meas}(\mathcal{P}X\times A,\mathcal{P}B)
for each
X
,
A
and
B
, and so a morphism
c^{\dagger}:\mathcal{P}Y\to\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{P})(X,Y)
equivalently has the type
\mathcal{P}Y\times X\to\mathcal{P}Y
. Paired with a channel
c:Y\to\mathcal{P}X
, we have something like a Cartesian lens; and to compose such pairs, we can use the Grothendieck construction
[
17
,
6
]
.

Definition 3.4

(Grothendieck lenses
[
6
]
)
.

We define the category
\mathbf{GrLens}_{F}
of Grothendieck lenses for a (pseudo)functor
F:\mathcal{C}\op\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}
to be the total category of the Grothendieck construction for the pointwise opposite of
F
. Explicitly, its objects
(\mathbf{GrLens}_{F})_{0}
are pairs
(C,X)
of objects
C
in
\mathcal{C}
and
X
in
F(C)
, and its hom-sets
\mathbf{GrLens}_{F}\big((C,X),(C^{\prime},X^{\prime})\big)
are given by dependent sums

\mathbf{GrLens}_{F}\big((C,X),(C^{\prime},X^{\prime})\big)=\sum_{f\,:\,\mathcal{C}(C,C^{\prime})}F(C)\big(F(f)(X^{\prime}),X\big)

(18)

so that a morphism
(C,X)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(C^{\prime},X^{\prime})
is a pair
(f,f^{\dagger})
of
f:\mathcal{C}(C,C^{\prime})
and
f^{\dagger}:F(C)\big(F(f)(X^{\prime}),X\big)
. We call such pairs
Grothendieck lenses
for
F
or
F\mathrm{\textit{-lenses}}
.

Proposition 3.5

(
\mathbf{GrLens}_{F}
is a category)
.

The identity Grothendieck lens on
(C,X)
is
\id_{(C,X)}=(\id_{C},\id_{X})
. Sequential composition is as follows. Given
(f,f^{\dagger}):(C,X)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(C^{\prime},X^{\prime})
and
(g,g^{\dagger}):(C^{\prime},X^{\prime})\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(D,Y)
, their composite
(g,g^{\dagger})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\circ$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\circ$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{1.1302pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.80728pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}}(f,f^{\dagger})
is defined to be the lens
\big(g\bullet f,F(f)(g^{\dagger})\big):(C,X)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(D,Y)
. Associativity and unitality of composition follow from functoriality of
F
. ∎

Example 3.6

(
\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}
)
.

Instantiating
\mathbf{GrLens}_{F}
with
F=\mathsf{Stat}:\mathcal{C}\op\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}
, we obtain the category
\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}
whose objects are pairs
(X,A)
of objects of
\mathcal{C}
and whose morphisms
(X,A)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Y,B)
are elements of the set

\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}\big((X,A),(Y,B)\big)\cong\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\times\mathbf{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(I,X),\mathcal{C}(B,A)\big)\,.

(19)

The identity
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lens}
on
(Y,A)
is
(\id_{Y},\id_{A})
, where by abuse of notation
\id_{A}:\mathcal{C}(I,Y)\to\mathcal{C}(A,A)
is the constant map
\id_{A}
defined in (
16
) that takes any state on
Y
to the identity on
A
. The sequential composite of
(c,c^{\dagger}):(X,A)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Y,B)
and
(d,d^{\dagger}):(Y,B)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Z,C)
is the
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lens }\big((d\bullet c),(c^{\dagger}\circ c^{\ast}d^{\dagger})\big):(X,A)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Z,C)
with
(d\bullet c):\mathcal{C}(X,Z)
and where
(c^{\dagger}\circ c^{\ast}d^{\dagger}):\mathbf{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(I,X),\mathcal{C}(C,A)\big)
takes a state
\pi:\mathcal{C}(I,X)
on
X
to the channel
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
. If we think of the notation
(\cdot)^{\dagger}
as denoting the operation of forming the Bayesian inverse of a channel (in the case where
A=X
,
B=Y
and
C=Z
), then the main result of this paper is to show that
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet\mathrm{d}^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
, where
\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}
denotes
(d\bullet c\bullet\pi)\text{-almost-equality}
(Definition
2.5
).

4
Bayesian lenses

We now show how to translate the categories of Grothendieck
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lenses}
defined above into the canonical profunctor optic form, thereby opening Bayesian lenses up to comparison and composition with other optics, and representation in the corresponding graphical calculi.

In order to give an optical form for
\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}
, we need to find two
\mathcal{M}\text{-actegories}
with a common category of actions
\mathcal{M}
. Let
\hat{\mathcal{C}}
and
\check{\mathcal{C}}
denote the categories
\hat{\mathcal{C}}:=\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\mathcal{C}\op,\mathbf{V})
and
\check{\mathcal{C}}:=\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\mathcal{C},\mathbf{V})
of presheaves and copresheaves on
\mathcal{C}
, and consider the following natural isomorphisms.

\displaystyle\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}\big((X,A),(Y,B)\big)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\times\mathbf{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(I,X),\mathcal{C}(B,A)\big)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{M\,:\,\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\times\mathcal{C}(X,M)\times\mathbf{V}\big(\mathcal{C}(I,M),\mathcal{C}(B,A)\big)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\times\hat{M}(X)\times\mathbf{V}\big(\hat{M}(I),\mathcal{C}(B,A)\big)

(20)

The second isomorphism follows by Yoneda reduction (
27
), and the third follows by the Yoneda lemma. We take
\mathcal{M}
to be
\mathcal{M}:=\hat{\mathcal{C}}
, and define an action
\odot
of
\hat{\mathcal{C}}
on
\check{\mathcal{C}}
as follows.

Definition 4.1

(
\odot
)
.

We give only the action on objects; the action on morphisms is analogous.

\displaystyle\odot:\hat{\mathcal{C}}

\displaystyle\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\check{\mathcal{C}},\check{\mathcal{C}})

(21)

\displaystyle\hat{M}

\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\hat{M}\odot-&:&\check{\mathcal{C}}&\to&\check{\mathcal{C}}\\
&&P&\mapsto&\mathbf{V}\big(\hat{M}(I),P\big)\end{pmatrix}

Functoriality of
\odot
follows from the functoriality of copresheaves. ∎

To confirm that
\odot
makes
\check{\mathcal{C}}
into a
\hat{\mathcal{C}}\text{-actegory}
, we need to check the actegory structure isomorphisms.

Proposition 4.2
.

\odot
equips
\check{\mathcal{C}}
with a
\hat{\mathcal{C}}\text{-actegory}
structure: unitor isomorphisms
\lambda^{\odot}_{F}:1\odot F\xrightarrow{\sim}F
and associator isomorphisms
a^{\odot}_{\hat{M},\hat{N},F}:(\hat{M}\times\hat{N})\odot F\xrightarrow{\sim}\hat{M}\odot(\hat{N}\odot F)
for each
\hat{M},\hat{N}
in
\check{\mathcal{C}}
, both natural in
F:\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\mathcal{C},\mathbf{V})
.

Proof.

We first check the unitor:

\displaystyle\lambda^{\odot}_{F}:1\odot\mathcal{C}(B,-)

\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}\big(1(I),\mathcal{C}(B,-)\big)

\displaystyle\cong\mathbf{V}\big(\mathbf{1},\mathcal{C}(B,-)\big)

\displaystyle\cong\mathcal{C}(B,-)

where
\mathbf{1}
is the terminal object in
\mathbf{V}
.

The associator is given as follows:

\displaystyle{a^{\odot}_{\hat{M},\hat{N},P}}^{-1}:\hat{M}\odot\left(\hat{N}\odot P\right)

\displaystyle=\mathbf{V}\left(\hat{M}(I),\mathbf{V}\left(\hat{N}(I),P\right)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathbf{V}\left(\hat{M}(I)\times\hat{N}(I),P\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathbf{V}\left((\hat{M}\times\hat{N})(I),P\right)

\displaystyle=(\hat{M}\times\hat{N})\odot P

where the first isomorphism follows by the Cartesian closure of
\mathbf{V}
.
∎

We are now in a position to define the category of abstract Bayesian lenses, and show that this category coincides with the category of
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lenses}
.

Definition 4.3

(Bayesian lenses)
.

Denote by
\mathbf{BayesLens}
the category of optics
\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}
for the action of the Cartesian product on presheaf categories
\times:\hat{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\hat{\mathcal{C}},\hat{\mathcal{C}})
and the action
\odot:\hat{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\check{\mathcal{C}},\check{\mathcal{C}})
defined in (
21
). Its objects
(\hat{X},\check{Y})
are pairs of a presheaf and a copresheaf on
\mathcal{C}
, and its morphisms
(\hat{X},\check{A})\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(\hat{Y},\check{B})
are abstract
Bayesian lenses
—elements of the set

\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}\Big((\hat{X},\check{A}),(\hat{Y},\check{B})\Big)=\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{M}\times\hat{Y})\times\check{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{M}\odot\check{B},\check{A})

A Bayesian lens
(\hat{X},\check{X})\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(\hat{Y},\check{Y})
is called a
simple
Bayesian lens.

Proposition 4.4
.

\mathbf{BayesLens}
is a category of lenses.

Proof.

The product
\times:\hat{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\hat{\mathcal{C}},\hat{\mathcal{C}})
on
\hat{\mathcal{C}}
is Cartesian, so
\mathbf{Comon}(\hat{\mathcal{C}})=\hat{\mathcal{C}}
. Hence

\displaystyle\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}\Big((\hat{X},\check{A}),(\hat{Y},\check{B})\Big)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{Y})\times\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{M})\times\check{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{M}\odot\check{B},\check{A})

(22)

is of the form in definition
2.15
.
∎

Proposition 4.5

(
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lenses}
are Bayesian lenses)
.

Let
\hat{(\cdot)}:\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\mathcal{C}\op,\mathbf{V})
denote the Yoneda embedding and
\check{(\cdot)}:\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\mathcal{C},\mathbf{V})
the coYoneda embedding. Then

\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}\Big((\hat{X},\check{A}),(\hat{Y},\check{B})\Big)\cong\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}\Big((X,A),(Y,B)\Big)

so that
\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}
is equivalent to the full subcategory of
\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}
on representable (co)presheaves.

Proof.

\displaystyle\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}\Big((\hat{X},\check{A}),(\hat{Y},\check{B})\Big)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{Y})\times\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{M})\times\check{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{M}\odot\check{B},\check{A})

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{Y})\times\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{M})\times\check{\mathcal{C}}\left(\mathbf{V}(\hat{M}(I),\check{B}),\check{A}\right)

\displaystyle\cong\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\times\hat{M}(X)\times\mathbf{V}\left(\hat{M}(I),\mathcal{C}(B,A)\right)

\displaystyle\cong\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}\Big((X,A),(Y,B)\Big)

The first isomorphism is just (
22
), the second obtains by definition of
\odot
, the third by the Yoneda lemma, and the fourth by (
20
).

Since Bayesian lenses are lenses, we can check diagrammatically that sequential composition in
\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\odot}
corresponds to that in
\mathbf{GrLens}_{\mathsf{Stat}}
. The composite lens
\innerproduct{d\:}{\: d^\dag}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\circ$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\circ$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{1.1302pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.80728pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}}\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
of
\innerproduct{d\:}{\: d^\dag}:(Y,B)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Z,C)
after
\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}:(X,A)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Y,B)
has the depiction

where the first expression is given by reading the right-hand side following the definition of optical composition (

); where the first isomorphism follows by the definitions of

,

, and the notation

We therefore have
\innerproduct{d\:}{\: d^\dag}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\circ$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\circ$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{1.1302pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.80728pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}}\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}\cong\innerproduct{d \klcirc c\:}{\: c^\dag\circ c^\ast d^\dag}
, which are just the components of the corresponding composite
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lens}
(Example
3.6
), and so
\mathsf{Stat}\text{-lenses}
are Bayesian lenses.
∎

Remark 4.6
.

We will often abuse notation by indicating representable objects in
\mathbf{BayesLens}
by their representations in
\mathcal{C}
. That is, we will write
(X,A)
instead of
(\hat{X},\check{A})
where this would be unambiguous.

It may be of interest sometimes to consider cases where the
\mathsf{update}
morphisms admit more or different structure to the
\mathsf{view}
morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
. We can generalize Bayesian lenses to such a mixed case as follows.

Definition 4.7
.

We first generalize the action
\odot
. Let
\mathcal{D}
be the category of
\mathsf{update}
morphisms. We assume it to be
\mathbf{V}\text{-enriched}
. We define an action
\oslash:\hat{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\check{\mathcal{D}},\check{\mathcal{D}})
of
\hat{\mathcal{C}}
on
\check{\mathcal{D}}
as a straightforward generalization of
\odot
as defined in (
21
). Once again, we give only the action on objects; the action on morphisms is analogous.

\displaystyle\oslash:\hat{\mathcal{C}}

\displaystyle\to\mathbf{V{\hbox{-}}Cat}(\check{\mathcal{D}},\check{\mathcal{D}})

\displaystyle\hat{M}

\displaystyle\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\hat{M}\oslash-&:&\check{\mathcal{D}}&\to&\check{\mathcal{D}}\\
&&P&\mapsto&\mathbf{V}\big(\hat{M}(I),P\big)\end{pmatrix}

\oslash
equips
\check{\mathcal{D}}
with a
\hat{\mathcal{C}}\text{-actegory}
structure, just as in Proposition
4.2
. We define a corresponding category of
mixed Bayesian lenses
as the obvious generalization of Definition
4.3
. Objects
(\hat{X},\check{Y})
are pairs of a presheaf on
\mathcal{C}
and a copresheaf on
\mathcal{D}
, and morphisms
(\hat{X},\check{A})\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(\hat{Y},\check{B})
are elements of

\mathbf{Optic}_{\times,\oslash}\Big((\hat{X},\check{A}),(\hat{Y},\check{B})\Big)=\int^{\hat{M}\,:\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}}\hat{\mathcal{C}}(\hat{X},\hat{M}\times\hat{Y})\times\check{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{M}\oslash\check{B},\check{A})\>.

Example 4.8

(State-dependent algebra homomorphisms)
.

Let
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(M)
be the Kleisli category of a monad
M:\Set\to\Set
and let
\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{E}\mspace{-3mu}\mathcal{M}(M)
be its Eilenberg-Moore category. Both
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
are
\Set\text{-enriched}
. A (representable) mixed Bayesian lens
\innerproduct{v\:}{\: u}:(S,T)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(A,B)
over
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
is then given by a Kleisli morphism
v:S\to MA
and an
S\text{-state-dependent}
algebra homomorphism
u:\Set\big(MS,\mathcal{E}\mspace{-3mu}\mathcal{M}(M)(B,T)\big)
. Under the forgetful functor
U:\mathcal{E}\mspace{-3mu}\mathcal{M}(M)\to\Set
and by the Cartesian closed structure of
\Set
,
u
is equivalently a function
u^{\flat}:MS\times B\to T
such that
u^{\flat}(\mu,-):B\to T
is an
M\text{-algebra}
homomorphism for each
\mu:MS
.

5
Bayesian updates compose optically

The categories of state-dependent channels and of Bayesian lenses defined in §
3
and §
4
are substantial generalizations of concrete Bayesian inversion as introduced in §
2.1
. In this section, we concentrate on the latter, noting that every pair of a stochastic channel
c
and its (state-dependent) inversion
c^{\dagger}_{(\cdot)}
constitutes a simple Bayesian lens
\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
satisfying the following definition. We adopt the terminology of ‘exact’ and ‘approximate’ inference
[
19
]
.

Definition 5.1

(Exact and approximate Bayesian lens)
.

Let
\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}:(X,X)\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}(Y,Y)
be a simple Bayesian lens. We say that
\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
is
exact
if
c
admits Bayesian inversion and, for each
\pi:I\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
such that
c\bullet\pi
has non-empty support,
c
and
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}
together satisfy equation (
8
). Simple Bayesian lenses that are not exact are said to be
approximate
.

We seek to prove the following theorem, which is the main result of this paper.

Theorem 5.2
.

Let
\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
and
\innerproduct{d\:}{\: d^\dag}
be sequentially composable exact Bayesian lenses. Then the contravariant component of the composite lens
\innerproduct{d\:}{\: d^\dag}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\circ$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\circ$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{1.61458pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{1.1302pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\circ$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.80728pt}{\scalebox{1.0}[0.33]{$|$}}$\crcr}}}}\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}\cong\innerproduct{d \klcirc c\:}{\: c^\dag\circ c^\ast d^\dag}
is, up to
d\bullet c\bullet\pi\text{-almost-}\allowbreak\text{equality}
, the Bayesian inversion of
d\bullet c
with respect to any state
\pi
on the domain of
c
such that
c\bullet\pi
has non-empty support. That is to say,
Bayesian updates compose optically
:
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
. Graphically:

(23)

Corollary 5.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}^{\dagger}
be the wide subcategory of channels in
\mathcal{C}
that admit Bayesian inversion (Definition
2.3
). Then
\mathcal{C}^{\dagger}
embeds functorially into
\mathbf{BayesLens}
. On objects, the embedding is given by
X\mapsto(\hat{X},\check{X})
; on morphisms,
c\mapsto\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
.

Because Bayesian inversion is only determined up to almost-equality, the embedding
\mathcal{C}^{\dagger}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{BayesLens}
is not unique, requiring a choice of inversion for each channel. However, in most situations of practical interest, there is a canonical choice. For those channels which have density function representations, the canonical choice is given by Proposition
2.8
or equation (
10
); alternatively, by restricting to finite support, Bayesian inversions are actually unique.

We supply proofs of Theorem
5.2
in various copy-delete categories at various levels of abstraction, starting with the concrete case of finitely-supported probability in
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
. We follow this with the most abstract case, in an arbitrary copy-delete category admitting Bayesian inversion (first without and then with density functions), followed then by the case of s-finite measures (with density functions), from which we also recover the discrete result.

For pedagogical purposes, the structure of this section mirrors that of §
2.1
, and we have attempted to structure the proofs to emphasize their commonalities.

5.1
Discrete case

In this section, we work in the category of stochastic channels
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
, described in §
2.1.1
. Note that with finite support, almost-equality reduces to equality, and so Bayesian inversions where they exist are unique.

Proof of Theorem
5.2
.

Suppose
p:X\to\mathcal{D}Y
and
q:Y\to\mathcal{D}Z
. Given a prior
\rho:1\to\mathcal{D}X
on
X
, we are interested in the Bayesian inversion
(q\bullet p)^{\dagger}_{\rho}:Z\to\mathcal{D}X
of
q\bullet p:X\to\mathcal{D}Z
with respect to
\rho
. Following (
5
), we have

\displaystyle(q\bullet p)_{(\cdot)}^{\dagger}

\displaystyle:\mathcal{D}X\times Z\to\mathcal{D}X

\displaystyle:=\rho\times z\mapsto\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\frac{(q\bullet p)(z|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{\sum_{x^{\prime}:X}(q\bullet p)(z|x^{\prime})\cdot\rho(x^{\prime})}}\,\ket{x}=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\frac{(q\bullet p)(z|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(q\bullet p\bullet\rho)(z)}}\,\ket{x}.

The lens composite of
q^{\dagger}
and
p^{\dagger}
with respect to
\rho
is
p^{\dagger}_{\rho}\bullet q^{\dagger}_{p\bullet\rho}
. Our task is therefore to show that

p^{\dagger}_{\rho}\bullet q^{\dagger}_{p\bullet\rho}(z)=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\frac{(q\bullet p)(z|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(q\bullet p\bullet\rho)(z)}}\,\ket{x}=(q\bullet p)^{\dagger}_{\rho}(z)\,.

By Kleisli extension (
4
), for any
\sigma:1\to\mathcal{D}Y
,

p^{\dagger}_{\rho}\bullet\sigma=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\sum_{y:Y}p^{\dagger}_{\rho}(x|y)\cdot\sigma(y)}\,\ket{x}=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\sum_{y:Y}\left(\frac{p(y|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(p\bullet\rho)(y)}\right)\sigma(y)}\,\ket{x}.

Now, let
\sigma\mapsto q^{\dagger}_{p\bullet\rho}(z)
, so

\displaystyle p^{\dagger}_{\rho}\bullet q^{\dagger}_{p\bullet\rho}(z)

\displaystyle=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\sum_{y:Y}\left(\frac{p(y|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(p\bullet\rho)(y)}\right)\cdot(q^{\dagger}_{p\bullet\rho})(y|z)}\,\ket{x}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\sum_{y:Y}\left(\frac{p(y|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(p\bullet\rho)(y)}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{q(z|y)\cdot(p\bullet\rho)(y)}{(q\bullet p\bullet\rho)(z)}\right)}\,\ket{x}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\sum_{y:Y}\frac{q(z|y)\cdot p(y|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(q\bullet p\bullet\rho)(z)}}\,\ket{x}

\displaystyle=\sum_{x:X}\,\boxed{\frac{(q\bullet p)(z|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{(q\bullet p\bullet\rho)(z)}}\,\ket{x}

\displaystyle=(q\bullet p)^{\dagger}_{\rho}(z)

as required.
∎

5.2
Abstract case

Here, we work in an arbitrary copy-delete category
\mathcal{C}
with those morphisms that admit Bayesian inversion in the abstract sense of equation (
8
) (§
2.1.3
). This proof implies the result in the more concrete categories
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
and
\mathbf{sfKrn}
; we include those for their computational and pedagogical content.

Proof of Theorem
5.2
.

Suppose
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}:Y\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
is the Bayesian inverse of

where the first obtains because
d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
is the Bayesian inverse of
d
with respect to
c\bullet\pi
, and the second because
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}
is the Bayesian inverse of
c
with respect to
\pi
. Hence,
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
and
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}
are both Bayesian inversions of
d\bullet c
with respect to
\pi
. Since Bayesian inversions are almost-equal (Proposition
2.9
), we have
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}
, as required.
∎

5.2.1
With density functions

Here, we work in an abstract copy-delete category
\mathcal{C}
in which stochastic channels can be represented by effects in the sense of Definition
2.4
(§
2.1.4
).

Proof of Theorem
5.2
.

Suppose

The last line follows by Lemma
2.10
, since the two almost-inverses
(p\mu q)^{-1}
and
q^{-1}
are
\nu\text{-almost}
equal (Proposition
2.7
).

We have shown that
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\overset{\nu}{\sim}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
. Recall that
d
is represented by an effect with respect to the state
\nu
. So by Lemma
2.11
, we have
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
, as required.
∎

5.3
S-Finite case with density functions

Here, we instantiate the abstract density function proof of §
5.2.1
in the category
\mathbf{sfKrn}
of s-finite kernels described in §
2.1.5
, in order to obtain a form of the result commensurate with the informal form of Bayes’ rule (
9
). Then, restricting to finitely supported measures, we recover the discrete case of the result in
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
.

Proof of Theorem
5.2
.

Equation (
10
) states that, by interpreting the string diagram of Proposition
2.8
for Bayesian inversion via density functions in
\mathbf{sfKrn}
, the Bayesian inverse
d^{\dagger}_{\rho}
of
d:Y\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}Z
with respect to
\rho:I\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}Y
is given by

\displaystyle d^{\dagger}_{\rho}:Z\times\Sigma_{Y}\to[0,\infty]:=z\times B

\displaystyle\mapsto\left(\int_{y:B}\rho(\mathrm{d}y)\,q(z|y)\right)q^{-1}(z)

\displaystyle=q^{-1}(z)\int_{y:B}q(z|y)\,\rho(\mathrm{d}y)

where
q^{-1}:Z\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}I
is a
\nu\text{-almost-inverse}
for
q\bullet((c\bullet\pi)\,\otimes\id_{Z})
, given up to
\nu\text{-almost-equality}
by

q^{-1}:Z\to[0,\infty]:=z\mapsto\left(\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\int_{x:X}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\right)^{-1}.

Suppose then that

\rho=c\bullet\pi:1\times\Sigma_{Y}\to[0,\infty]:=\ast\times B\mapsto\int_{y:B}\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\int_{x:X}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\,.

We therefore have, by direct substitution,

\displaystyle d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}:Z\times\Sigma_{Y}\to[0,\infty]:=z\times B

\displaystyle\mapsto q^{-1}(z)\int_{y:B}q(z|y)\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\int_{x:X}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x).

We now write down directly the Bayesian inverse of the composite channel,
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}:Z\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
:

\displaystyle(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}:Z\times\Sigma_{X}\to

\displaystyle[0,\infty]

\displaystyle:=z\times A\mapsto

\displaystyle\left(\int_{x:A}\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\,(p\mu q)(z|x)\right)(p\mu q)^{-1}(z)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(p\mu q)^{-1}(z)\int_{x:A}(p\mu q)(z|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(p\mu q)^{-1}(z)\int_{x:A}\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)

where
(p\mu q)^{-1}
is a
\nu\text{-almost-inverse}
for
(p\mu q)\bullet(\pi\otimes\id_{Z})
, or equivalently (since almost-inverses are almost-equal; Proposition
2.7
), a
\nu\text{-almost-inverse}
for
q\bullet((c\bullet\pi)\,\otimes\id_{Z})
.

The lens form of the inverse composite is
c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}:Z\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
, and we follow the diagrammatic reasoning to show that this is equal to the direct form above:

\displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}:Z\times\Sigma_{X}\to

\displaystyle[0,\infty]

\displaystyle:=z\times A\mapsto

\displaystyle\,\int_{y:Y}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}(A|y)\cdot(d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi})(\mathrm{d}y|z)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\,\int_{y:Y}\left(p^{-1}(y)\,\int_{x:A}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\right)\cdot\left(q^{-1}(z)\,q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,\int_{x:X}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\,\int_{y:Y}\left(p^{-1}(y)\,\int_{x:X}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\right)\cdot\left(q^{-1}(z)\,q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,\int_{x:A}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)\right)

\displaystyle\overset{\mu}{\sim}

\displaystyle\,q^{-1}(z)\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\int_{x:A}p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\,q^{-1}(z)\int_{x:A}\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,p(y|x)\,\pi(\mathrm{d}x)

\displaystyle\overset{\nu}{\sim}

\displaystyle\,\big((d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\big)(A|z)

The second equality follows by Fubini’s theorem in
\mathbf{sfKrn}
(equivalently, by the symmetry of the monoidal product
\otimes
; see §
2.1.5
), and the last line by Lemma
2.10
since almost-inverses are almost-equal (Proposition
2.7
); compare the final part of the graphical proof in §
5.2.1
. Finally, by Lemma
2.11
, we have
(d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\overset{d\bullet c\bullet\pi}{\sim}c^{\dagger}_{\pi}\bullet d^{\dagger}_{c\bullet\pi}
, also as in §
5.2.1
.
∎

Corollary 5.4
.

By restricting to finitely supported measures, we recover the discrete-case result of §
5.1
.

Proof.

Suppose then that the prior
\pi:I\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
is represented by a density function
\rho:X\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}I
with respect to a measure
\upsilon:I\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}X
. Suppose further that the measures
\mu
,
\nu
, and
\upsilon
are finitely supported. Then

\displaystyle\big((d\bullet c)^{\dagger}_{\pi}\big)({x}\,|\,z)

\displaystyle=q^{-1}(z)\int_{x:\{x\}}\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,p(y|x)\,\upsilon(\mathrm{d}x)\,\rho(x)

\displaystyle=\frac{\int_{x:\{x\}}\int_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y)\,p(y|x)\,\upsilon(\mathrm{d}x)\,\rho(x)}{\int_{y^{\prime}:Y}q(z|y^{\prime})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}y^{\prime})\int_{x^{\prime}:X}p(y^{\prime}|x^{\prime})\,\upsilon(\mathrm{d}x)\,\rho(x^{\prime})}

\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,p(y|x)\,\rho(x)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}:Y}q(z|y^{\prime})\sum_{x^{\prime}:X}p(y^{\prime}|x^{\prime})\,\rho(x^{\prime})}

Now, assume that the density functions are indeed probability densities (
i.e.
, they sum to 1 over their support), and note that they are therefore functions of the form
X\times Y\to[0,1]
. We therefore recognise them as stochastic matrices
X\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\displaystyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\textstyle\raisebox{0.77496pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptstyle\raisebox{0.54247pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\rightarrow$\crcr$\scriptscriptstyle\raisebox{0.38748pt}{\scalebox{0.66}{$\bullet$}}\,$\crcr}}}Y
in
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
, and can interpret the foregoing expression as

\frac{\sum_{y:Y}q(z|y)\,p(y|x)\,\rho(x)}{\sum_{y^{\prime}:Y}q(z|y^{\prime})\sum_{x^{\prime}:X}p(y^{\prime}|x^{\prime})\,\rho(x^{\prime})}=\frac{\big(q\bullet p\big)(z|x)\cdot\rho(x)}{\big(q\bullet p\bullet\rho\big)(z)},

where
\bullet
is now composition in
\mathcal{K}\mspace{-2mu}\ell(\mathcal{D})
, thereby recovering the result in the discrete case.
∎

6
Lawfulness of Bayesian lenses

The study of Cartesian lenses substantially originates in the context of bidirectional transformations of data in the computer science and database community
[
5
,
1
]
, where we can think of the
\mathsf{view}
(or
\mathsf{get}
) function as returning part of a database record, and the
\mathsf{update}
(or
\mathsf{put}
) function as ‘putting’ a part into a record and returning the updated record. In this setting, extra structure known as
lens laws
can be imposed on lenses to ensure that they are ‘well-behaved’ with respect to database behaviour. Well-behaved and ‘very well-behaved’ lenses in the database context roughly correspond to our notion of ‘exact’ Bayesian lens, but as we will see, even exact Bayesian lenses are only weakly lawful in the database sense.

We will concentrate on the three lens laws that have attracted recent study
[
1
,
15
]
:
GetPut
,
PutGet
, and
PutPut
. A Cartesian lens satisfying the former two is
well-behaved
while a lens satisfying all three is
very well-behaved
, in the terminology of
[
5
]
. Informally,
GetPut
says that getting part of a record and putting it straight back returns an unchanged record;
PutGet
says that putting a part into a record and then getting it returns the same part that we started with; and
PutPut
says that putting one part and then putting a second part has the same effect on a record as just putting the second part (that is,
\mathsf{update}
completely overwrites the part in the record). We will express these laws graphically, and consider them each briefly in turn.

Note first that we can lift any channel
c
in the base category
\mathcal{C}
into any state-dependent fibre
\mathsf{Stat}(A)
using the constant (identity-on-objects) functor taking
c
to the constant-valued state-indexed channel
\rho\mapsto c
that maps any state
\rho
to
c
. We can lift diagrams in
\mathcal{C}
into the fibres accordingly.

GetPut

.

\innerproduct{c\:}{\: c^\dag}
is said to satisfy the
GetPut
law if it satisfies the left isomorphism in (
24
) below. Equivalently, because the copier induced by the Cartesian product is natural (

Note that by Bayes’ law, exact Bayesian lenses only satisfy
GetPut
with respect to states. This result means that, if we think of
c
as generating a prediction
c\bullet\pi
from a prior belief
\pi
, then if our observation exactly matches the prediction, updating the prior
\pi
according to Bayes’ rule results in no change.

.

The reason
PutGet
fails to hold in general is that Bayesian updating by construction mixes information from the prior and the observation, according to the strength of belief. Consequently, updating a belief according to an observed state and then producing a new prediction need not result in the same state as observed; unless, of course, the prediction already matches the observation.

PutPut

Finally, the
PutPut
law for a lens
\innerproduct{v\:}{\: u}
is characterized by the following isomorphism:

u
u
u
\cong

PutPut
fails to hold for exact Bayesian lenses for the same reason that
PutGet
fails to hold in general: updates mix old and new beliefs, rather than entirely replace the old with the new.

Comment

The lens laws were originally defined in the context of computer databases, where there is assumed to be no uncertainty: database logic is Boolean (database instances are objects in a presheaf topos
[
4
]
), so a ‘belief’ is either true or false. Consequently, there can be no ‘mixing’ of beliefs; and in database applications, such mixing may be highly undesirable (putting epistemological concerns aside). Bayesian lenses, on the other hand, live in a fuzzier world: the present author’s interest in Bayesian lenses originates in their application to describing cognitive and cybernetic processes such as perception and action, and here the ability to mix beliefs according to uncertainty is desirable.

Possibly it would be of interest to give analogous information-theoretic lens laws that characterize exact and approximate Bayesian lenses and their generalizations; and we might then expect the ‘Boolean’ lens laws to emerge in the extremal case where there is no uncertainty and only Dirac states. We leave such an endeavour for future work: Bayes’ law (
8
) is sufficiently concise and productive for our purposes here.

7
